title: Hubble Image of NGC 3324
caption: The edge of the NGC 3324 cavity in the Carina Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 3324 · constellation Carina · about 7,200 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA); Acknowledgment: N. Smith (University of California, Berkeley)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Dark towers of cool gas and dust climb above a glowing wall of gas, set against a soft blue background and trailed by wispy tendrils. This is the rim of a giant cavity inside NGC 3324, a star-forming region at the northwest corner of the Carina Nebula, roughly 7,200 light-years away in the constellation Carina.

Intense ultraviolet light and stellar winds from several hot, young stars hollowed out the cavity. A cluster of extremely massive stars at the center of the nebula, well outside this frame, ionizes the gas and keep digging the cavity deeper. Where the gas is densest, at the tops of the towers, it holds out against the radiation, so each tower points along the direction in which the energy flows. Elsewhere the wall is slowly being worn away.
NASA released the picture to mark ten years of the Hubble Heritage Project, launched in October 1998 to share some of the telescope's most attractive pictures with the public.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded light from hydrogen in 2006, and Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 added light from sulfur and oxygen in 2008. Sulfur is shown in red, hydrogen in green and oxygen in blue.
understand.eye: Each filter isolates the glow of a single gas and the colors are assigned to tell them apart, while about 2 hours of exposure gather far more light than an eye could.

explore: The Carina Nebula complex, also cataloged as NGC 3372, also holds the Keyhole Nebula and Eta Carinae, an active star prone to outbursts. Over the years the Heritage team has worked with several of Hubble's optical cameras, including WFPC2, which replaced the original Wide Field Planetary Camera in 1993, and the newer Advanced Camera for Surveys, which was also used here.
